Inside WildDogTV

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
They bring you the wilddog hunts, hyena cubs, penguins mating - unadulterated wildlife, we dive behind the actions of WildDogTV to see how they survived covid, and are making conservation magic.

Unique Selling Point:
We will be inside their home to see what life is like for them behind the scenes. They bring live videos to a paying audience - but that money goes towards conservation. They have done elephant collarings, wild dog translocations, snare removals... owned by Brent Leo-Smith (whose father is the legendary kevin leo-smith) he saw other platforms that make a profit from bringing facebook lie videos, and decided that that could be put to good use as a conservation funding tool. Enter the Endangered Wildlife Trust who has several people who work side-by-side with Brent's team.

Summary:
THEIR MOTTO: "PUSHING THE BOUNDARIES OF WHAT IT MEANS TO BE A WILDLIFE MEDIA COMPANY." They allow massive corporates to pay big money for private and exclusive virtual tours, and it's been a big success. These have paid for the collerings, the vet bills, much needed equipment etc so its not just entertainment but giving back to the animals in the big picture. It's also tech heavy with over 30 years of combined conservation, safari industry and film-making experience, while based in the wild heart-land of South Africa bordering the famous Kruger National Park. They have found new ways of filming and placing live cameras so that the exclusive audience can have unfettered access.

Living in the house together is: BRENT LEO-SMITH (presenter, tour guide, co-owner), WIUM DÖRNBRACK (co-owner, tech whizz), CHARLES COLLOCOTT (accountant and CFO), KHAYA TLOU (presenter and tour guide), YUKA OTA (presenter and tour guide from japan), MATTHEW GIE (camera operator and editor), BRYAN JOUBERT (editor, camera man). We will see them living in the house, how they get along and make it work!

Further information:
Founded in January 2019 by Brent Leo-Smith and Wium Dörnbrack. Brent and Wium’s over 30 years of combined wildlife, conservation, and film-making experience has helped them guide Painteddog.tv to achieving some remarkable feats in a surprisingly short time. After having established the Painteddog.tv as wildlife documentary film-makers and the “go-to” wildlife media film-crew in South Africa’s Lowveld region during 2019, in 2020 the company developed unique live broadcast capabilities during covid 19 which allowed us to achieve the following world firsts during that year:

Live elephant collaring in the Greater Kruger National Park
Live rescued painted dogs release into a protected reserve
Live painted dog collaring in the Greater Kruger National Park
Private & corporate live virtual safaris in the Greater Kruger National Park
24 hour live-streaming wild hyena den camera

Extra Budget Items:
we are going to have two nights there as flights are at midday sadly, and we are taking floris the editor with. SO it will be flights and stay for three.

Script:


INTRO: It’s the bush - but with a twist: raw... fascinating… deadly… With viewers able to immerse themselves in the scenes of survival playing out in the wild.
Brent: This is definitely a first for me.I am never going to forget this interview. You're surrounded by lions. Brent, how did we get here?
Well, a long road for Point dog tv, to be sitting here with you..
Brent Leo-Smith founded Painted Dog TV which now live streams interactive safari experiences from Hoedspruit in the Greater Kruger. His subscribers, or pack members, join the game drives from the comfort of homes all over the world.
Brent: You don't have to sort of tap, tap, tap, type your questions. You can have a conversation with your guide. You can have a joke with your guide.
So most of our game drives, we have a maximum of 10 to 12 people and you can actually talk physically to your guide.
This wasn’t always the business model they had in mind: what started as a service for international film crews was forced in a different direction when Covid struck. Like so many other businesses it was a case of “sink or swim”.
Brent: We hadn't quite perfected the virtual safari equipment yet, during the first lockdown, the game drives, we could only go like 150 metres. So because we didn't have that equipment that enabled us to sort of extend the range. Fortunately, like with anything, when there's problems and whatnot, it's how you look at them and how you handle them. We managed to make stuff out of what was available in country
TECH link: WHEN YOU THINK OF THE BUSH YOU THINK - NO SIGNAL, HERE WE HAVE STATE OF THE ART TECH, BEST SERVICE IN… WHILE BEING CONNECTED TO THE WORLD…
This is possible thanks to Engineer and Co-founder Wium Dornbrack.
Wium: It was rough in the beginning, we had no signal. a lot of the tech we use is coming from the gaming scene tech and all just combine it in our own little recipe area.
Wium: there was no internet access, no nothing. So we had to build out our own internet network So we found the biggest trees on the hills and we placed all our antennas on there and spray painted them.
The result is what the team now calls a “treepeater…” (instead of repeater)
LINK: THERE WE HAVE IT - INTERNET connectivity FROM THE BUSH.
Brent: We launched a subscription base where people could pay for exclusive content. And from that, I think it was probably two 300 people who was supporting us monthly. ee managed to sort of pinch and save and get our first car, which is the one we're sitting on now. The Badger. 38 years young.
Isn't that your age?
We're the same age group. We are both nineteen eighty three models.
Keeping my own vintage to myself, I chatted to subscribers during a game drive…
MASA asks questions of virtual subscribers!
Khaya Tlou is one of their guides and hosts a show exploring the week's best videos “Find My name is Khaya, last name Tlou”
Masa: You speak eight languages, but I also hear that you also speak bird?
Kt: (bird sounds)
Masa: I just heard it.
Kt: (bird sounds)
Masa: And what can you mimic? (bird sounds)
Khaya:I have a love of the bush that’s incalculable.I’m different. Other guides wear brown socks and clothes…
Khaya also has - shall we say - some unusual food preferences.
Masa: I heard you also eat poo?
kt: Yeah, but you have to be careful, it tastes nice for me, you know its just grass. The one that I eat a lot and most elephant poop laughing….
But what’s the secret of this startup's success?
Brent: Well, we still don't take salaries for three years now. We made a very conscious decision not to go to the banks and not to borrow money. So we've self-funded the thing completely.
And the cost saving doesn’t end there - the 10 person crew have become housemates with each playing a role in the company. So they work and live in this home called the “oasis…”
So these are live bush cameras and they actually spread out all over southern Africa or South Africa at the moment…
…from penguin peepholes to spy cams in private reserves…
We all live on site because, I mean, most mornings starts at about four o'clock.
Editor and cameraman Bryan Joubert is always ready for action.
It's not a normal stock standard day because sometimes you have to run out for an elephant coloring or a wild dog coloring, this lifestyle suits me. It's good for me as well. I'm a bit of a hermit, so it forces me to socialize.
A hermit he may be, but his guest-appearing thumb has become a celebrity “I have 2000 people following my thumb…”
Charles: It's philosophically very rewarding to be able to work with nature as opposed to a lot of businesses where you often working against nature.
CFO and accountant Charles Collocott quit his job in Johannesburg to answer the call of the wild.
e I'm the chief pencil pusher here. Brent calls these my sandton hands, because they have very little scars and calluses on them. And so I do all the numbers and the paper and all the rest.
As its newest member, Director Keshnie Govender found leaving home for the first time challenging.
To be out with a pride of lions and then a huge breeding herd of elephants, that is an incredible and awesome all. You were there, so you would understand that it was a magical experience and it reminded me of why I'm here and why I've left my parents and my family and my, my comforts and my lifestyle back at home.
And she’s still adjusting to the dress code.
But I mean, just wearing white today, I get a little bit of bush shamed, all white in the bush.,
Cameraman and editor Matthew Gie shows us their memory wall… (You’re live)
there's me on a makgoro (zambia) and you can see the landscape in the background.
Brent and i are there filming during a sunset and then the photo right next to it as well? That's me.
But there’s more to this than building memories and subscribers - the need to protect the animals they spend their days observing is a key focus.
Brent: At the same time, when we do do those events, they directly raise money for the conservation organizations we're working with. We're launching a conservation travel as well.(Oh, here comes another lioness..). You can join us virtually or you can join us in person. And part of that safari is that you actually spend time with the scientists or the researchers from the different conservation organizations.
In just one example, R120 000 has so far been raised for NGO, the Endangered Wildlife Trust. Grant Beverley is part of its carnivore programme.
Grant So we've saved a pack of wild dogs that had roamed outside of protected areas and were coming into conflict with a commercial farmer. carnivores are I regard it as as keystone species because by protecting them you indirectly conserving the environment that they live in.
The hard realities of the tension between humans and nature are evident in the work of Brent and his colleagues.
Brent: One of my biggest issues with a lot of the wildlife content and whatnot that's around is that it's not honest that they're hard, the hard part and everything's beautiful But it doesn't talk about the hardships of the people and the animals. I would just like South Africans to fall in love with our wildlife and our country as much as we do and become ambassadors for these incredible animals and make sure that they're protected for future generations.
